newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia spruces up capital for Taylor inauguration.
newsitem.headline: Liberia spruces up capital for Taylor inauguration.

text.p: Hundreds of Liberians and peacekeeping troops with bulldozers worked frantically on Friday to complete a facelift to Liberia's war-battered capital in readiness for its first presidential inauguration for 12 years.

President-elect Charles Taylor, a converted warlord, is expecting for Saturday's ceremony about a dozen heads of state ranging from Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha and Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi to Laurent Kabila of Democratic Republic of the Congo.
South African sources said President Nelson Mandela would be represented by his Interior Minister Mangosuthu Buthelezi.

"Most of them will arrive on Saturday morning for the ceremony and leave immediately afterwards because accommodation and other facilities to ensure their comfort are simply non-existent," said a hotel owner involved with preparations.

Taylor led last-minute preparations, including redecoration of the inaugural venue -- the Centennial Hall erected in central Monrovia 50 years ago on the 100th anniversary of the founding of Liberia by freed American slaves.

Streets in the the city centre, bustling again after the devastation caused by militia warfare and massive looting in April-May 1996, are festooned with Liberia's national flag -- the Lone Star -- a modest copy of the U.S. Stars and Stripes.
Work gangs repainted walls of the dilapidated Executive Mansion, the seafront officce and residence presidential complex over which faction leaders fought a bitter seven-year war.
Liberians seeking to close a horrific chapter in their national history opted for strong leadership by voting massively for Taylor -- the man who started the conflict in December 1989.
The widows of Liberia's last two presidents from the descendants of freed slaves -- William Tubman and William Tolbert -- will witness the ceremony, organisers said.
Tolbert, the last of the so-called Americo-Liberian presidents, was killed in a 1980 coup led by then sergeant Samuel Doe, who became the last elected president in 1985.
Doe's alleged rigging of those elections precipitated the chain of events leading to the civil war in which he was captured by guerrillas and tortured to death in September 1990.
Taylor will be the first Americo-Liberian leader since 1980.
The Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force, ECOMOG, which has been policing Liberia since 1990 and provided security for the elections has promised a trouble-free inauguration.
"Adequate steps have been taken to ensure the safety of everyone," one ECOMOG commander told Reuters.
A task force of ECOMOG troops and police has been clearing kiosks from main Monrovia streets and the 35-km (20-mile) highway leading to the Robertfield International Airport.
Meanwhile, Taylor has announced his main cabinet nominations, putting a key guerrilla ally in charge of defence but offering jobs to a handful of former rivals.

In a 15-man cabinet announced on Thursday night, Taylor named former guerrilla commander Peter Chea as defence minister. He kept Monie Captan and Bonnoh Jallah respectively at foreign affairs and justice from the outgoing transitional government.

Taylor also retained former militia rival and stalwart of the Krahn tribe Roosevelt Johnson as transport minister. The commerce portfolio went to Bangali Fofana, an ally of another ex-warlord, Alhaji Kromah, a losing presidential candidate.
No job has yet gone to supporters of former United Nations executive Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, Taylor's distant runnerup in the presidential election and the only woman candidate.
Confirmation of the appointments by parliament should be routine. Taylor's National Patriotic Party won 21 of the 26 Senate seats and 49 of the 64 in the House of Representives.
He swept the presidency with over 75 percent of votes.
